label: Abstract Algebra
shortDescription: A free abstract algebra course covering groups, rings, fields, homomorphisms, and an introduction to Galois theory.
modulesDescription: Read the abstract algebra chapters in order, or jump directly to the topic you need.
ogTitle: Learn Abstract Algebra for Free | CalcPath
ogDescription: Free university abstract algebra course. Groups, homomorphisms, rings, fields, factorization, and Galois theory — with practice problems and full worked solutions.
courseDescription: Free university-level abstract algebra course covering the fundamentals of groups, rings, fields, and an introduction to Galois theory. Master the structural language of modern mathematics with hundreds of practice problems with step-by-step solutions.

topics.title: Groups
topics.description: The group axioms and what they force: uniqueness of the identity and inverses, cancellation, the reversal rule for inverses, and the Cayley table as a Latin square; orders of elements with ord(a^k) = n/gcd(n,k); cyclic groups classified as Z or Z/nZ, with the Klein four-group showing abelian does not imply cyclic; worked throughout in Z/nZ, the unit groups, S_3, the dihedral groups and GL_2.

topics.title: Subgroups, Cosets, and Quotient Groups
topics.description: The one-step and two-step subgroup tests; cosets proved to partition a group into equal blocks, and Lagrange's theorem proved from that partition with Euler and Fermat as corollaries; four equivalent characterisations of normality; quotient groups proved well defined exactly when the subgroup is normal; group actions, orbit-stabiliser and the class equation; and the Sylow theorems with applications to groups of small order.

topics.title: Group Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms
topics.description: Homomorphisms and what they preserve; the kernel proved normal and every normal subgroup realised as a kernel; injectivity equivalent to a trivial kernel; the first isomorphism theorem with its well-definedness spelled out, then the second, third and correspondence theorems; Cayley's theorem; and the automorphism group, with Inn(G) = G/Z(G) and Aut(Z/nZ) = (Z/nZ)^*.

topics.title: Rings
topics.description: The ring axioms and the arithmetic they force; the units as a group and why a unit is never a zero divisor; finite rings where every non-zero-divisor is a unit; the subring criterion and the centre; characteristic, forced to 0 or prime in a domain; and the binomial theorem with the freshman's dream giving the Frobenius map. Unit groups computed for Z/nZ, matrix rings, polynomial rings, the Gaussian integers and the quaternions.

topics.title: Ideals and Quotient Rings
topics.description: Ideals and the absorption property that makes quotient multiplication well defined; Z and F[x] proved principal via the division algorithm; kernels of ring homomorphisms are exactly the ideals; the first isomorphism theorem for rings and the correspondence theorem; R/P a domain iff P is prime and R/M a field iff M is maximal, both directions; and the Chinese Remainder Theorem for comaximal ideals.

topics.title: Integral Domains and Fields
topics.description: Cancellation as the defining feature of a domain; every field is a domain and every finite domain is a field, by a pigeonhole argument; characteristic 0 or prime, the prime subfield, and finite fields of order p^n; the Frobenius endomorphism; and the field of fractions constructed in full, with the well-definedness checks that are where the domain hypothesis is spent.

topics.title: Polynomial Rings and Unique Factorization
topics.description: Degrees add over a domain, and what breaks without it; the division algorithm, remainder and factor theorems, and the bound on the number of roots; Euclidean domains are PIDs and PIDs are UFDs, with a separating example at each gap in the containment chain; irreducible and prime coinciding in a PID; and irreducibility testing by Gauss's lemma, the rational root theorem and Eisenstein's criterion.

topics.title: Field Extensions and Galois Theory
topics.description: Field extensions and the tower law proved via the product basis; algebraic elements, minimal polynomials and splitting fields; the Galois group with |Gal| = [K:F] exactly for normal separable extensions; the fundamental theorem as an inclusion-reversing correspondence, worked completely for Q(sqrt2,sqrt3) and for the splitting field of x^3-2; finite and cyclotomic extensions; ruler-and-compass impossibility by degree; and solvability by radicals with Abel-Ruffini.
